new_statements.quote: (5) Dynamic accent (accompanied by high or falling tone) plays a far bigger part in grammar than syllable pitch. Bari retains distinct traces of inherent tone, but it is safe to predict that soon all these languages will be entirely stress-languages and not tone-languages in the Sudanic sense.
new_statements.citation: Tucker, A. N. 1935. Survey of the language groups in the Southern Sudan. Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies (University of London) 7(4): 861-896 -- closing section 'Analysis of the Nilo-Hamitic Languages', p. 891, point (5) (re-report of A's work 0 for a passage A did not mention).
new_statements.locator: p. 891, 'Analysis of the Nilo-Hamitic Languages', point (5); scanned the text layerof the copy consulted
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.relation_note: Family-level typological impression: in the Nilo-Hamitic languages dynamic (stress) accent, accompanied by high or falling tone, does more grammatical work than syllable pitch; inherent (lexical) tone survives in traces (Bari named); Tucker predicts these languages will become pure stress languages. No stress-placement rule, no language-by-language detail, nothing on any Lotuko dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule; claims grammatical (not lexical) use of a dynamic accent realised with high/falling pitch across the Nilo-Hamitic groups, with residual lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Bari 'retains distinct traces of inherent tone'.
new_statements.identity_note: The passage generalises over Tucker's whole 'Nilo-Hamitic' division (Bari group, Lotuko group, Topotha-Turkana group, Masai, Nandi-Tatoga); the Lotuko group as he defines it (pp. 886-887) includes the Lango dialects incl. Madial (= Lorwama area) and, after Driberg, the Lokathan/Bira (= Ketebo), so Okolie falls under its scope only by classification. Tucker had no Ketebo/Lorwama (indeed no dialect-level Lotuko) prosodic data; the remark reflects Bari, Lotuko proper, Masai, Nandi. Not usable as an okol1243 statement; recorded so the passage is not rediscovered as one.

sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey only (200-item wordlist lexicostatistics, RTT, EGIDS, attitudes). Gives autonym Okolie [òkólíɛ̀], Ketebo [kɛ̀tɛ́bò], Lorwama [lòɾwámá]; Ketebo~Lorwama 90% lexically similar, next closest Dongotono 46-47%. No prosody statement.

sources.citation: Vossen, Rainer. 1982. The Eastern Nilotes: Linguistic and Historical Reconstructions (Kölner Beiträge zur Afrikanistik 9). Berlin: Reimer. -- Rosetta Project excerpt for Dongotono [ddd], pp. 165-166.
sources.note: Nothing on Okolie; excerpt is informant notes for Dongotono/Lokoya. Vossen collected no Ketebo/Lorwama data (his Lotuxo-group languages are Lotuko, Lopit, Dongotono, Lokoya).

sources.note: Nothing on Lorwama/Ketebo accent. Says Dongotono and Lorwama are mutually intelligible, not intelligible with Lotuxo proper, lack the Lotuxo gender prefix, show Acoli lexical influence. Muratori's accent section (sec. 49, p. 18) concerns Lotuxo proper only.
